overview: Cherokee history includes distinct southeastern communities and continuing nations in Oklahoma and North Carolina. Writing, newspapers, basketry and food knowledge record achievements made by individuals and families as well as governments. Forced removal devastated communities, but Cherokee people rebuilt institutions and maintained connections to their homelands.

periods.title: Constitution and bilingual printing
periods.summary: The Cherokee Nation adopted a written constitution in 1827. The Cherokee Phoenix followed in 1828, printing Cherokee and English at New Echota. These institutions developed while the Nation faced mounting pressure on its land.

periods.title: Forced removal
periods.summary: United States troops and state militias rounded up Cherokee people in 1838. Detention and forced journeys broke up households and caused deaths. This phase concerns removal, not an end to Cherokee existence.

periods.title: Rebuilding and distinct continuing nations
periods.summary: The Cherokee Nation adopted a new constitution in 1839 and rebuilt at Tahlequah amid serious internal conflict. Cherokee Nation, the United Keetoowah Band and the Eastern Band have distinct governmental histories; one institution cannot stand for all Cherokee people.

sections.title: A writing system becomes a printed public voice

items.text: Sequoyah developed a syllabary for writing Cherokee. In 1825 the Nation commissioned English and Cherokee type for a press. Adapting a writing system to movable type connected linguistic invention with practical publishing equipment and organization.

The first Cherokee Phoenix appeared at New Echota on 21 February 1828. Its Cherokee and English columns made the same newspaper accessible across languages. Surviving issues are material evidence of Cherokee authorship and political communication before removal.

Publication continued in a new setting with the Cherokee Advocate, established in Tahlequah in 1844. It printed both languages as the Nation rebuilt schools, homes, businesses and government buildings after removal.

A rivercane basket from the Qualla Boundary, catalogued as 15/8659, was collected in 1927 or 1928. The museum records its twill-plaited construction but does not name its maker. The collection date should not be mistaken for the year it was woven.

Lottie Queen Stamper recalled her family making white-oak baskets after work in the fields. Preparing splints required carefully splitting wood into usable strips. Her recollection connects an admired finished object to seasonal farm work and demanding preparation.

Stamper expanded into rivercane and plant dyes, then recorded patterns in notebooks and on graph paper for students. Teaching changed how designs circulated between families and materials while preserving close attention to technique.

In 1940, Stamper studied a photograph of an older double-weave basket held in Britain and worked out its pattern. Other Cherokee elders still knew this technique. Her achievement strengthened its teaching; describing her as the sole rediscoverer would erase those weavers.

Eastern Cherokee speaker Tommy Cabe describes gathering sochan greens with relatives in spring and later teaching his own children. His account includes care for the plant and gratitude before picking. It documents one living family tradition in its own voice.

Cherokee Nation offers immersion education in Tahlequah, online teaching and a master-apprentice language program. Different ways of learning connect children and adults with speakers, continuing the language beyond what any historic printed page can preserve.

In May 1838, federal troops and state militias began forcing Cherokee families into detention. People often had little time to collect possessions. Subsequent travel by roads and waterways brought further hardship, illness and death.

The 1839 constitution was part of rebuilding, but it did not immediately resolve conflicts between earlier western migrants, removal supporters and those forced west. A new government should not be mistaken for an uncomplicated recovery from dispossession.

Cherokee Nation and the United Keetoowah Band are based in Oklahoma; the Eastern Band is based in North Carolina. Each has its own government and citizenship system. The broad label Cherokee on this map includes histories that need these distinctions.

ending.text: United States removal policies caused enormous loss of life, homes and land. They did not end Cherokee peoples or political life. Cherokee Nation, the United Keetoowah Band and the Eastern Band continue as distinct nations; the map's eighteenth-century endpoint describes only its available historical coverage.
